extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general literate public interested in early-18th-century periodical essays and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting prescriptive norms and evaluative principles embedded in early-18th-century Spectator essays and letters (social rules, literary taste, moral conduct). This covers periodical-essay style, social precedence, and moral-ethical guidance present in the collected numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedency of books and authors (folio vs octavo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary / publishing precedence: the author notes established ceremonial rules that determine precedence among writers and their works — e.g., 'six Octavo's have at all times been look'd upon as an Equivalent to a Folio.' The writer expects to take rank after several volumes are gathered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains social/publishing metric: accumulated smaller works (multiple octavos) can equal the standing of a larger folio; printers and booksellers 'take the Wall of one another, according to the abovementioned Merits of the Authors to whom they respectively belong.' Used to justify author's future claim to precedence after publishing several volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank among the learned professions and social classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A table of social precedence places the three Learned Professions above the general illiterate class (Squires): 'this last Order of Men being the illiterate Body of the Nation, are consequently thrown together into a Class below the three Learned Professions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance is social/normative rather than procedural: the author remarks that rural squires sometimes usurp precedence but their want of learning 'may in some measure extenuate their Misdemeanour' and that learned men 'ought to pardon them.' Intended as etiquette for seating/rank in learned society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedency among actors and dramatic writers (stage maxim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage and literary precedence rules: 'a Tragedian always takes place of a Comedian' and 'Once a King, and always a King.' Queens and Heroines preserve rank in private conversation; waiting-women and maids of honour keep distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends to writers of drama: 'all Writers of Tragedy look upon it as their due to be seated, served, or saluted before Comick Writers' with tragi-comedy authors between them. Notes long disputes (e.g., between Tragick and Heroick Poets) and customary deference (burlesque to heroic, comic to serious). Presented as the 'Table of Laws' that preserves order in the 'Republick of Letters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Veneration and reverent use of the Divine Name
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral/style standard: maintain habitual worship and veneration of the Supreme Being and avoid using God's name on trivial occasions; using it in ordinary expressions of anger, mirth, or ludicrous phrases is 'prevailing Impiety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples and appeals to authority (Bishop Burnet's remark about Boyle's reverence; Jewish practice of avoiding the name). Strong admonition: using the divine name in jokes, everyday exclamations, or perjuries is an affront to reason and religion. Framed as both inward piety and outward linguistic decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approach to diminutive epithets in poetry (Adrian's lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary-interpretive criterion: treat Latin diminutives like 'vagula, blandula' as expressions of endearment and concern, not necessarily levity; consider literary usage (Catullus and hendecasyllabic poets) and contextual factors (a dying man's meditation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: diminutives convey tenderness and seriousness in such contexts; critics should weigh historical and genre conventions (classical usage) and the poet's situation (deathbed reflection) before deeming lines trivial. Offers the specific interpretive reading of Adrian's lines as 'a very serious Soliloquy to his Soul.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote merit: critics' duty to foster good works
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethos for editors/critics: be 'studious to produce other Men's Merit' and 'zealous in promoting the Fame and Welfare of the Praise-worthy.' Turn personal ambition into supporting good productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by concrete acts: extorting excellent productions from reluctant authors, animating young gentlemen into worthy pursuits, and undermining 'the Interests of Ignorance, Vice, and Folly' in favour of 'Learning, Piety, and good Sense.' Presented as a deliberate editorial/cultural policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of effective moral and satirical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive criterion for laudable writing (from poetic praise): spotless thoughts, precepts that 'please while they cure,' satire that reforms ('Lash'd in thy Satire, the penurious Cit / Laughs at himself'), and works that encourage learning, virtue, and public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the praise-poem: writing that teaches without shocking, that reforms readers by witty self-recognition, that promotes learning (members quit vices and take up study), and that addresses grand themes (Fame, Heaven, Hell) while also pleasing. Implies that good periodical writing combines moral aim with agreeable form and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility and protection of modest company in public travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral/moral standard for public conduct: indecent or lewd discourse directed at (especially female) passengers in public conveyances is condemned as severely as other public assaults—presented as a form of persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative example: account of young officers subjecting a modest woman to indecent talk on a coach; proposed remedies (satirical) include a padlock for the mouths of impertinent fellows and a proclamation protecting modest persons. Framed as an appeal to public decency and gentlemanly behaviour.
